We have carbon NMR shifts: 135.80, 117.40, 70.50, 54.00, 43.70 ppm. Need to determine number of CH3 groups in the compound. Use carbon shifts to infer functional groups. Typical chemical shift ranges: methyl carbons (sp3) around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic; but if attached to heteroatoms shift higher: e.g., O-CH3 ~55 ppm; N-CH3 ~40-50 ppm; carbonyl attached methyl (acetyl) ~20-30 ppm; aromatic carbons ~120-150 ppm.

Given shifts: 135.8, 117.4 (aromatic sp2), 70.5 (likely carbon attached to O, maybe CH2O or CH-O), 54.0 (likely O-CH3), 43.7 (likely N-CH3 or maybe CH2 attached to N). So there are at least two methyl groups: O-CH3 (methoxy) and N-CH3 (dimethyl? but only one shift). Could be one methyl attached to O (54 ppm) and one attached to N (43.7). So count = 2.

But need to be sure: Could 43.7 be a CH2? CH2 attached to N maybe ~40-50. But CH2 would have 2 hydrogens, not methyl. However we only need CH3 groups. The 54 ppm is typical for O-CH3 (methoxy). The 43.7 could be a carbon attached to N but could be CH2. However CH2 attached to N is around 40-45. So ambiguous. Could be CH3 attached to N (N-CH3) also around 40-45. Without further data (e.g., DEPT), we can't differentiate. But likely there are two methyls.

We could also get proton NMR to confirm number of methyl signals. Let's request proton NMR.
